name: Closest hedge to a target
brief:
A book holds positions with signed sizes, in lots, in no particular order. A trader wants two different positions whose sizes add up as close as possible to `target`.

Write `closest_pair_gap(sizes, target)`, which returns the smallest value of `abs(sizes[i] + sizes[j] - target)` over positions `i != j`.

Example. For `sizes = [8, -3, 5, 12, -7]` and `target = 3`, the pair -3 and 5 sums to 2. No pair sums to exactly 3, so the answer is 1.
constraints: $2 \le n \le 100{,}000$ sizes, each a whole number between $-10^9$ and $10^9$.
$O(n \log n)$ time is the target. Checking every pair is too slow.
All the tests in a run share one 5-second limit in the browser.
hint: Sort a copy first. Then put one pointer at each end. If the sum is too small, the left pointer must move right; if too big, the right one moves left.

examples.note: -3 and 5 make 2, one away from the target.
The only pair hits the target, so the gap is 0.

tests.call: closest_pair_gap([3 * i for i in range(100000)], 299990)

how: Submit runs 13 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value.
notes: After sorting, the pair sum moves in one direction when either pointer moves, so one sweep sees every useful pair.
A size cannot pair with itself: the pointers stop when they meet, and a single 3 is no hedge for a target of 6.
The sort costs $O(n \log n)$ and the sweep $O(n)$.

planted.slip: It binary searches the partner for each size but lets a position pair with itself, so a lone size can look like a perfect hedge.
